overview.body:
**Arete** ​(*arete*) — ‌Excellence, Virtue ‌· The ​highest ​fulfillment of ​aretē — ​belongs ​to the ‌Greek tradition, ​where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Excellence, Virtue". ​The ‌name means ​"Excellence, virtue"[^1].

​**Arete** ​is the ​Greek personification ​and concept ‌of ​excellence, virtue, ‌and the ​fulfilment of ‌a ​thing's proper ‌function. For ​a ‌knife, arete ​is sharpness; ​for a ‌horse, ‌speed; for ‌a human ​being, the ​full ‌development of ​mind, body, ​and ‌character. The ​word carries ​no single ‌English ​equivalent: it ‌means virtue, ​but also ​skill, ​courage, moral ​goodness, and ‌simply ‌being the ​best version ‌of what ​one ​is.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Arete** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/arete/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*arete* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 7.53-77 (Arete, queen of the Phaeacians).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Ἀρετή**. Etymologically ​it ​means ​"Excellence, virtue"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII form ​*arete* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Arete** ‌recovers ​the full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**a** ​→ **A** ‌— ‌A ​uppercase
- **r** ‌→ ​**r** — ​r ‌same
- **e** ‌→ ‌**e** — ‌e ​same
- **t** ‌→ ​**t** — ​t ​same
- **e** ‌→ ​**e** ​— e ​same

‌Attested and ​derived ​spellings of ​the ‌name:

- **Aretḗ** ​— ‌ideal form: ​Stacked ‌macron+acute on ​the ‌stressed long ‌vowel, ​matching ​Greek Ἀρετή; ​philologically ​ideal but ‌often ‌untypeable on ​phones.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/a.rɛː.tɛː/** — ​Attic Greek ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**a-** — ‌Short alpha ​[a], the ​unstressed first ‌syllable of ​the name.
- ‌**-rē-** — ​Long epsilon ‌[ɛː], written ​eta (η), ​the middle ​syllable that ​carries weight.
- ​**-tē** — ‌Long epsilon ​[ɛː], written ‌eta (η), ​with the ‌acute pitch ​accent on ‌the final ​syllable.

‌For the ​modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ‌'ah-ray-TAY' — ‌the final ​syllable carries ​the pitch ‌and is ​long; the ​middle vowel ‌is also ​long.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ​the name:

- ‌**Greek** — ​Ἀρετή (Arete), ​excellence, virtue, ​the fulfilment ​of a ‌thing’s proper ‌function
- **Latin ​equivalent** — ‌virtus, manly ​courage and ​moral excellence
- ‌**PIE (disputed)** ‌— Traditionally ‌connected ‌with *h₂er- ​“to fit ‌together” — ​Greek ἄρτιος ​“fitting,” Latin ​ars “skill,” ‌English art; ​Beekes judges ​the prehistory ​uncertain.

The ‌Greek Ἀρετή ​contains both ​stress (acute ​on the ‌final eta) ​and length ‌(both middle ​and final ‌vowels are ​long eta), ‌making it ‌a full ​restoration. The ​plain ASCII ​arete loses ​both the ‌accent and ‌the vowel ​length.

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is written ‌in ​Greek ​as **Ἀρετή**. ​This ​original ​script ‌is the ​form ​against ‌which the ​ASCII ‌fallback ​*arete* ‌and the ​PuniCodex ​restoration ​**Arete** are ​measured: ​the ‌restoration ​preserves its ‌full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ‌written ​form, ‌so that ​a ​reader ‌typing the ‌modern ‌address ​still ​speaks the ‌ancient ​name.[^1]

​The name ‌is ​written ​in ‌Greek as ​**Ἀρετή**. ‌The ​final ​eta carries ​the ​acute ‌accent and ‌is ​long; ‌the ​middle eta ​is ‌also ‌long. The ‌plain ‌ASCII ​*arete* ‌flattens both ​the ​pitch ​accent and ‌the ​vowel ​length. ​The PuniCodex ‌restoration ​**Arete** ​preserves the ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of ‌the Greek ​form ‌and ​is classified ‌as ‌a ​full ​restoration because ​both ​stress ‌and length ‌are ​present.

domains.body:
**Arete** ​is ‌the Greek ‌personification ​and ​concept of ​excellence, ​virtue, ​and ‌the fulfilment ​of ​a ‌thing's proper ​function. ‌For ​a ‌knife, arete ​is ​sharpness; ​for a ​horse, ​speed; ‌for ​a human ‌being, ​the ‌full development ​of ‌mind, ​body, ‌and character. ​The ​word ‌carries no ‌single ‌English ​equivalent: ​it means ‌virtue, ​but ​also skill, ‌courage, ​moral ​goodness, ‌and simply ​being ‌the ​best ​version of ​what ​one ‌is.[^1]

### Excellence

‌The ​quality ‌of ​performing one's ​function ‌to ‌the highest ‌degree.

### ‌Virtue

​Moral ‌and civic ​goodness, ​the ​habit of ‌choosing ​rightly.

### ​Courage

​The arete ‌most ​praised ​by Homer: ​the ‌willingness ​to ‌face danger ​for ‌a ​worthy end.

### ‌Wisdom

‌For ​Plato ​and Aristotle, ​the ​highest ‌arete is ‌intellectual ​virtue.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 7.53-77 (Arete, queen of the Phaeacians).

mythology.body:
Arete is more concept ​than character, but Greek mythology dramatised her ‌in one famous scene: Prodicus' allegory of Heracles ‌at the crossroads. There the young hero ​must choose between two women, one representing ​Arete and the other Kakia (Vice). The choice ​shaped every later Western telling of the ​hero's education.[^1]

### Heracles at the Crossroads (Prodicus)

​The sophist Prodicus of Ceos told it, and ‌Xenophon preserved it (Memorabilia 2.1.21–34): the founding ​myth of Greek moral education. The young ​Heracles, at the threshold of manhood, sat alone ‌in a quiet place, torn, when two ​tall women approached. One was beautiful, modest, ‌her eyes cast down, dressed in white: Arete. ​The other was fed to plumpness, her ‌eyes bright, her skin painted, dressed to ​be seen: Kakia, Vice. Kakia spoke first — ​a short road to every pleasure, “no ​mention of toil.” Arete answered: “I dwell ​with the gods… nothing good comes to mortals ​without toil and sweat”; she promised labor ‌first, then honor, and fame that outlives ​the grave. Heracles took her hand. Prodicus ends ‌with Vice objecting that her rival offers ​nothing but sweat — and Arete answering: ‌“you would know better had you ever done ​anything noble.” The allegory means virtue makes ‌her case in full knowledge that she ​will lose the argument on comfort.[^2]

### Arete in ‌the Odyssey (Homer)

In the Odyssey 7.53–77, ​Arete is also a queen — the ​wife of Alcinous, ruler of the seafaring Phaeacians, ‌and daughter of his brother Rhexenor. Homer ‌lavishes rare detail on her: her hand ‌on the household, her mediation of disputes, the ​people’s love (“as a god she is ​honored in the land”). When the shipwrecked ‌Odysseus begs for passage home, Athēnē instructs him ​to pass the king and fall at ​the queen’s knees — for her favor ‌decides the matter; Nausicaa had said it plainly ​(6.303–315), her mother is the power in ​the house. Whether the queen’s name is ‌the common noun made flesh or simply a ​well-chosen aristocratic one, Homer lets her live ‌the meaning: **arete as the excellence of ​judgement and hospitality that actually governs**. It means ​the word was never only a soldier’s ​virtue.

### Aristotle’s Virtue (Philosophy)

Aristotle made arete ​the load-bearing wall of Western ethics (Nicomachean Ethics ‌I–II, VI). Human beings, like every thing, ‌have an ergon — a function: the ​activity of the rational soul. The arete of ‌a thing is whatever lets it perform ​its function well; so the arete of ​the eye is seeing, of a horse running, ‌of a human being **rational activity in ‌accordance with virtue**. Virtue itself he locates ‌in the will: a hexis, a settled disposition, ‌“a mean between extremes, determined by reason” ​— courage between rashness and cowardice, generosity ‌between waste and meanness. The goal is eudaimonia, ​flourishing, which is activity of the soul ​expressing arete. The doctrine means morality is ​a skill: not a gift or a rule-book ‌but a trained excellence, acquired exactly as ​a weaver or a lyre-player acquires one.

### ​The Only Good (Stoicism)

The Stoics drew the ​sharpest line of all: arete is the ‌only good (Diogenes Laertius 7.89–98, summarizing Stoic ​ethics). Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself are ​“indifferents” — preferred, but not good; their ​opposites are indifferents too, only dispreferred. Only ‌wisdom, justice, courage, and self-control count, because only ​they are always beneficial and always within ‌our power. The sage who possesses arete ​is free in the chains-and-kings sense: no tyrant ‌can take from her the one thing ​that is genuinely hers. Epictetus, himself enslaved, ‌taught that the door to freedom is the ‌judgement that externals are nothing; Marcus Aurelius, ​an emperor, wrote the same doctrine from ​the other end of the social world, rehearsing ​each morning the indifference of palaces and ​shacks alike. The doctrine means virtue ethics’ ‌oldest claim in its purest form: **the good ‌life is the one thing the good ​person can never lose**.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 7.53-77 (Arete, queen of the Phaeacians).

archaeology.body: Personified ​Arete enters ‌Greek ‌art in ​the later ​fifth ​century BCE ​— ​a draped ‌woman ​labelled ΑΡΕΤΗ ​on Attic ‌and ​South Italian ‌vases ​— and ‌the ​Romans minted ​her counterpart ​Virtus ​on imperial ​coinage, ‌the standing ​female ‌with spear ​and ‌shield. The ​Choice of ‌Heracles ​became a ‌favorite ​of Roman ​floor ‌mosaicists: surviving ‌examples from ‌Antioch ​and the ​western ‌empire (second–third ​century ​CE) show ‌the two ​women ​flanking the ‌hero, ​Arete with ‌her ​hand raised ​in argument ​— ​the sophist’s ‌debate ‌staged in ​household ‌stone. On ​the Greek ​mainland ‌the word ‌itself ‌is the ‌monument: ​honorific decrees ‌and epitaphs ​across ​the Aegean ​praise ‌individuals “for ​their ​aretē,” so ​the ‌abstraction survives ​less in ​temples ​than in ‌thousands ​of inscribed ‌stones. ​Arete’s civic ‌shrine is ​lexical ‌— the ‌culture ​agreed with ​Aristotle ​that the ​city exists ‌to ‌make excellence ​possible.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 7.53-77 (Arete, queen of the Phaeacians).
Plato, Republic (arete of the soul and the city).

meditation.body:
Arete ​asks ‌us ‌what we ​are ​for. ​The ​question ​sounds ‌strange ​to modern ​ears, ‌because ​we ‌tend ​to ‌think ​of human ​beings ​as ​self-creating ​rather ‌than ​as ‌having a ​function. ‌But ​the ‌Greek ​concept ‌is more ​flexible ​than ‌it ‌first ‌appears: ​arete ​is not ‌a ​single ​recipe ‌but ​the ​question ‌of how ​this ‌person, ​in ​this ​situation, ​can ‌act excellently.

‌To ​pursue ‌arete ​is ​to ‌accept ‌that excellence ‌has ‌a ​cost. ‌The ​road ​is steep, ​the ‌training ​is ​long, ​and ‌the ​temptations of ​ease ​are ‌constant. ​Yet ‌the ​alternative ‌is not ​freedom ‌but ‌a ​failure ​to ​become ​what one ‌could ‌have ​been.[^1]
